name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,377

clue.text: Tear in injured part of eye (6)

indicators.note: something injured is damaged out of its proper shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A medical note about a tear in an injured eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Tear in' a rip in something injured, and 'injured part of eye' reads as one phrase; in fact 'injured' works on the two words before it and the definition is only 'part of eye'.
explanation.definitionFit: The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

indicators.note: to forget PEN is to leave those letters out of the name

blocks.note: the letters removed from the front of PENELOPE

explanation.surface: Someone runs off with a girl and leaves their pen behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flee with girl' is almost a definition of eloping on its own, which is the joke; the girl is PENELOPE, and dropping PEN leaves ELOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: To elope is to run away secretly, usually to marry.

indicators.note: to wind is to twist, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Hellish, smoky winds, as if blowing from the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winds' looks like a noun going with 'smokier'; it is a verb, pronounced to rhyme with 'finds'. 'Infernal' is used in its everyday sense of annoying, not hellish.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Infernal' in everyday speech means maddening, as in 'that infernal noise', which is what irksome means.

blocks.note: a timber named after the tree it comes from

explanation.surface: A plain statement that timber leaves something behind when burnt.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings sit side by side as one sentence, so it reads as 'wood leaves ash'; each half is a definition in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is both a hardwood tree and the residue of burning.

clue.text: Building for animals far from rickety (6)

blocks.note: a farm building where horses are kept

explanation.surface: An animal shed that is solidly built.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings join into a single description of a sturdy barn; one is a noun, the other an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A stable is a building for horses, and stable also means firmly fixed.

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are remade

explanation.surface: Asked whether the hungriest person gets to cook, the reply is an eager yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as question and answer in a kitchen; the answer to the question is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Sure thing!' is a casual way of saying 'certainly!'.

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above, so AN sits on top of GEL

blocks.note: to gel is to set, as a jelly does

explanation.surface: A prop or article placed on a film set, perhaps a statue of a cherub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests an item, and 'set' a stage set; the article is the grammatical word AN and set is the verb GEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: cherubs, the winged infants of religious art, are one order of heavenly messenger.

clue.text: European is entertained by attraction in free time (7)

indicators.note: a guest who is entertained is taken in, so E and IS go inside LURE

blocks.note: a lure is something that attracts

explanation.surface: A European tourist being hosted by a local attraction on their day off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is not a link word here: it supplies its own two letters, and the surface's host-and-guest picture is exactly the container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: hours away from work are free time.

blocks.note: a steelmaking city in the English county of Yorkshire; read as a place, it names the county
the surface wants metal; the setter means steel as inner toughness, and 'perhaps' flags a synonym by example

explanation.surface: A reference to the steel for which Sheffield is famous.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheffield is a city in Yorkshire, in northern England, famous for steelmaking. Here steel means resolve, as in 'nerves of steel', and Yorkshire folk are proverbially known for grit.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit and steel both mean toughness of character, and Sheffield is in Yorkshire, so a Sheffielder's steel is Yorkshire grit.

explanation.surface: Someone checking whether an old embargo still applies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old embargo' reads as one phrase; 'old' belongs to the wordplay and only 'embargo' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are official bans stopping something from going ahead.

blocks.note: a flask is a kind of bottle

explanation.surface: Stashing a hip flask up high where no one will find it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drinker hiding a flask on a high shelf; 'Hide' is the definition in the sense of suppressing feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: feelings kept corked like liquid in a flask are hidden from others.

indicators.note: after means following in sequence, so the letters for running come behind those for perfect

blocks.note: a machine that is on is running

explanation.surface: A wicked streak of running after a perfect game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect game' looks like a sporting phrase, but 'perfect' is MINT and 'game' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Badminton is a racket game played with a shuttlecock.

clue.text: Scatter drapes all over the place (6)

indicators.note: things all over the place are in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Curtains flung untidily around a room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scatter' could equally read as a command to fling the drapes about; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean distributing things widely over an area.

clue.text: Rapt, if a novel is sweet (7)

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new form

explanation.surface: A reader wonders whether being absorbed in a novel is a pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book to be rapt in; it is the adjective meaning new. 'Sweet' is the noun, a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A parfait is a frozen or layered dessert, and a sweet is a dessert.

clue.text: Favourite pushed back by inches, part of a foot (6)

indicators.note: by means next to, so TEP stands beside INS

blocks.note: INS is the abbreviation for inches
a teacher's pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: A favourite shoved back a few inches, like a runner edged out of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the favourite first, but 'by' lets the inches come first in the answer; order in the clue need not be order in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the arched top of the foot between toes and ankle.

indicators.note: sprinkled things are scattered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman has spilt talcum powder in her bag.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a powder spill in a handbag; 'in' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a school bag carried on a shoulder strap.

explanation.surface: Something first-rate is falling to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-class; 'cracking' is British slang for excellent, as in 'a cracking good read'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracking means both excellent and splitting apart.

clue.text: Shade of pink right within something black (5)

indicators.note: within means inside, so the letter for right sits inside the black thing

explanation.surface: A pinkish tint showing inside something black.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something black' is deliberately vague: the setter wants the stock black thing of crosswords, a fuel, rather than a colour word like ebony or jet.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral is a pinkish-orange colour.

indicators.note: something rolled over is turned end to end, so ABUT is read backwards

blocks.note: things that abut touch each other

explanation.surface: A player rolling over and bumping into their instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touch' reads as a verb applied to the instrument; it is ABUT, which turned round gives TUBA.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the big bass brass of a band.

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so take the last letter of bean

blocks.note: the brow of a hill is its top

explanation.surface: The best cocoa bean, in the end, makes chocolate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top bean' reads as the finest bean; 'Top' is BROW, and 'chocolate' is the colour, not the sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: chocolate names a deep shade of that colour, as in a chocolate Labrador.

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Waterproof hats wrecked by someone careless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyed without thinking' reads as careless damage; the definition is only 'without thinking'. Learning parrot fashion is repeating by rote, a mostly British phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeat something parrot fashion is to say it mechanically, without thinking about its meaning.

clue.text: Every other bit of carpet fitting (3)

indicators.note: take every second letter of carpet

explanation.surface: A carpet fitter who covers only every second patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet fitting' reads as one trade; 'fitting' is the definition in the sense of suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adjectives mean suitable for the occasion.

clue.text: Slur about leader in loathsome old dictator (6)

indicators.note: the leader of loathsome is its first letter

blocks.note: a slur or stain on someone's reputation

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a hateful former tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader in loathsome' looks like 'a leader who is loathsome'; it is just one letter, and the tyrant only appears in the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union as a dictator until 1953.

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thank you, what you say on receiving a present

explanation.surface: A present that was only lent, which the giver should not have handed over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have!' is what people say when thanked with a present, so it stands for TA, British slang for thanks. The surface makes 'Gift' a present; it is a natural ability.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of a natural ability, as in 'a gift for languages'.
